# Numbers 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview / Context

Numbers 17 follows immediately after the rebellion of Korah (ch. 16). God had already vindicated Aaron through the plague stopped by his atoning censer, but He now provides an additional, gracious miracle to settle the question of the priesthood publicly and permanently.

> **Technical Note:** Numbers 17:1 in English Bibles is 17:16 in the Hebrew text (BHS). From 16:36 through 17:13 the English and Hebrew verse numbers differ, realigning at 18:1 (Precept Austin, citing NET notes).
> https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-17-commentary

---

## v. 1 — "And the LORD said to Moses…"

The Lord speaks to Moses, "presumably upon the same day" as the events of chapter 16, since the design was to prevent any recurrence of the sin and punishment just witnessed (Pulpit Commentary). Bush adds that the miracle was worked "while the minds of the people were yet in an excited state," since every divine judgment has a merciful intention toward survivors — to inspire salutary fear and prevent similar iniquities.
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm
https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-17-commentary

Gilbrant notes: the two previous plagues had defended Aaron from attack, but God now performed "a gracious miracle by which he would once and for all publicly designate Aaron as high priest." It may have appeared to some that Moses was simply keeping the priesthood in the family; this miracle would directly show God's choice.
https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-17-commentary

---

## v. 2 — "Take from them twelve staffs, one from the leader of each tribe. Write each man's name on his staff."

The Hebrew word for rod/staff is *matteh*, used over 200 times in the OT, most often translated "tribe." It is the same word for Moses' shepherd's staff (Exodus 4:2), later called "the staff of God" (Exodus 4:20) — the symbol of authority by which Moses performed miracles in Egypt and parted the Red Sea. The rod was a fitting instrument for God to display His miraculous creative power and demonstrate which owner was chosen to bear His authority as high priest (Precept Austin / Bush).
https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-17-commentary

The Pulpit Commentary explains that each tribe was "but a branch, or rod, out of the stock of Israel, and therefore was most naturally represented by the rod cut from the tree." The princes who brought rods must be those named in chapters 2 and 7 — including Ephraim and Manasseh as separate tribes — so the twelve rods were exclusive of Aaron's.
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

Matthew Henry notes: "It is probable that they were the staves which the princes used as ensigns of their authority; old dry staves, that had no sap in them."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/numbers/17.htm

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary observes: each prince brought his rod with his tribe's name inscribed; "the kind of tree from which the rods were cut is not known, except in the case of Aaron's rod. It was from an almond tree." The test was appropriate: "each tribe was but a 'rod' or branch of the parent stock, Israel. As each branch was cut off from the parent stem, there was no life in it… God would demonstrate His selection by giving life to His choice."
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-17.html

**Question of twelve or thirteen rods:** The Pulpit Commentary and Haydock both discuss this. Haydock notes that Origen (Homily 9) and most others hold there were 13 rods, since the tribe of Joseph was divided into Ephraim and Manasseh, each with its own prince. But some infer only 12 rods from the phrase "Aaron's rod was in the midst of their rods." Enduring Word notes both views exist (Cole = 12 total; Poole = 12 plus Aaron's).
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/17.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

---

## v. 3 — "Write Aaron's name on the staff of Levi, because there must be one staff for the head of each tribe."

There was no tribe prince of Levi. The Pulpit Commentary says this rod was therefore "provided by Moses himself, and inscribed by him with the name of Aaron, who stood by Divine appointment … above all his brethren." For Levi, there must be not three rods (for the three Levite sub-tribes) but one bearing Aaron's name as their common superior.
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains why Aaron's name and not simply "Levi": "The name of Aaron rather than of Levi was used, as the latter name would have opened a door of controversy among the Levites; and as there was to be one rod only for the head of each tribe, the express appointment of a rod for Aaron determined him to be the head of that tribe, as well as that branch or family of the tribe to which the priestly dignity should belong."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/17.htm

James Smith, in Handfuls of Purpose (cited at Precept Austin), draws a devotional point: "Only one out of the twelve yielded up rods were chosen. Yes. But which was chosen? The one with the High Priest's name on it." The application: consecrate yourself in the Name of Jesus Christ, the Great High Priest, and your life will bud, blossom, and yield fruit.
https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-17-commentary

---

## v. 4 — "Place the staffs in the Tent of Meeting in front of the Testimony, where I meet with you."

"Before the testimony" means in front of the ark containing the two tablets of the law (Pulpit Commentary). Several commentators debate whether the rods were placed inside the Holy of Holies or just outside the veil. Enduring Word notes that some (Allen, Cole) believe they were in the Most Holy Place, while others suggest just outside the veil.
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

James Smith (Precept Austin) draws an application: "Each representative had to be ENTIRELY YIELDED UP. Each rod was to be 'laid up before the testimony.' Put in the holy place, in front of the veil. Those who would have the Divine impression stamped upon them must be wholly yielded up to Him."
https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-17-commentary

---

## v. 5 — "The staff belonging to the man I choose will sprout, and I will rid Myself of the constant grumbling of the Israelites against you."

God promised that the chosen man's rod would blossom — a miraculous sign. The Hebrew verb for "make to cease" (*hashikkoti*) means "I will cause to sink so that they shall not rise again" (Pulpit Commentary). The blossoming of dead wood spoke of fruitfulness: "Fruitfulness – miraculous fruitfulness – is present when godly authority and leadership are being practiced" (Enduring Word / Guzik).
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

Guzik also observes: "Murmurers (complainers) are rarely satisfied by evidence or the resolution of one issue. Complainers are usually not issue-motivated, though they may claim to be and appear to be. More often they are heart-motivated." God would give unmistakable evidence, then "rid Himself" of the complaints — meaning He would no longer regard them but would judge them.
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

---

## v. 6 — "So Moses spoke to the Israelites, and each of their leaders gave him a staff… twelve staffs in all. And Aaron's staff was among them."

The Pulpit Commentary notes a significant detail: Moses did not keep Aaron's rod separate (which might have caused suspicion), but let it be seen among the others.
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

Haydock's Catholic Commentary similarly notes from the Hebrew: "the rod of Aaron was in the midst of their rods" — ensuring no suspicion of tampering.
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/17.htm

---

## v. 7 — "Then Moses placed the staffs before the LORD in the Tent of the Testimony."

"Before the Lord" — i.e., in front of the ark. The phrase "tent of the testimony" (*ohel ha'edut*) designates the tabernacle as the place where God's covenant witness resided (Pulpit Commentary).
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

---

## v. 8 — "The next day Moses entered… and saw that Aaron's staff… had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds."

This is the central miracle of the chapter. The Pulpit Commentary gives a rich exposition:

- The rod "was budded" (*parach* — sprouted). It "yielded almonds" — more precisely, "matured almonds."
- This particular rod had been cut from an almond tree. It probably displayed shoots, flowers, and fruit simultaneously — all stages of natural growth exemplified together.
- The almond's Hebrew name *shaked* means "awake," because it is the first tree to awake from winter sleep. Jeremiah 1:11 uses the "rod of an almond tree" as a symbol of God's vigilant haste to fulfill His purposes.
- The miracle was a *sēmeion* — a sign that was also a parable. "Aaron's rod could no more blossom and fruit by nature than any of the others, since it also had been severed from the living tree; and so in Aaron himself was no more power or goodness than in the rest of Israel. But as the rod germinated and matured its fruit by the power of God… even so in Aaron the grace of God was quick and fruitful."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

**Enduring Word (Guzik)** emphasizes that God gave far more evidence than necessary: a small green sprout would have sufficed, but God provided buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds — "many infallible proofs." He cites Wenham: "We are probably to understand that some parts were in bud, others in bloom and others had fruited." Allen: "Miracles in the Bible are often of this sort: natural events in unnatural conditions, timing, and placement."
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

**Pett's Commentary** notes that the word for "blossoms" (*tsits*) is the same word used for the golden "plate" on the High Priest's headdress (Exodus 28:36; Leviticus 8:9). It also connects almonds (*shaked*) with vigilance (*shoked*) from Jeremiah 1:11-12. Thus: the budding = new life; the flowers = high priestly "holiness to Yahweh" in whiteness of purity; the almonds = Yahweh watching over him with vigilance.
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/numbers-17.html

**Ellicott's Commentary** draws the Christological connection: "As the budding of Aaron's rod was the divinely appointed proof of the establishment of the priesthood in his person and in his posterity, so our Lord proved Himself to be the true High Priest over the House of God by coming forth as 'a rod [or shoot] out of the stem of Jesse' (Isaiah 11:1), and as 'a root out of a dry ground' (Isaiah 53:2)."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/17.htm

**Dr. Constable's Expository Notes**: "The message was clear: just as God could make an apparently dead rod miraculously bear fruit, so he could elect a line of descendants like any other and enable it to render priestly service fruitfully."
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-17.html

**Guzik** also stresses: "God's choice of Aaron's rod did not mean that Aaron was the most spiritual man in the nation… this wasn't a contest to determine the most spiritual man among them." It also did not mean Aaron had not or would not sin; it meant he was God's appointed priest and the nation must recognize it.
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

### Denominational / Traditional Differences on v. 8

**Catholic (Haydock / Challoner):** The rod of Aaron "was a figure of the blessed Virgin conceiving and bringing forth her Son, without any prejudice to her virginity." The logic: just as a dry rod could produce fruit without receiving moisture from the earth, so Mary could become a mother without losing her virginal integrity. This typology is traced to St. Augustine, St. Gregory of Nyssa, and St. Bernard. Additionally, the rod is a figure of Christ's passion and glorious resurrection (Origen, Homily 9). St. Ambrose: "The grace of the priesthood never fades." The almond tree — the first to blossom — is styled a "watching rod" (Jeremiah 1:11).
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/17.htm

**Reformed (Ligonier):** The significance of Aaron's rod is found in God's sovereign choice. "The Lord then caused Aaron's rod to bud as a sign that He had indeed chosen Aaron as His priest. The rod was placed in the ark to demonstrate God’s sovereign choice of the priestly mediator between man and God, the ultimate fulfillment of this role being achieved in Jesus Christ (Heb. 5:4)." The ark as a whole (manna, rod, tablets) is "a picture of the person and saving work of Christ."
https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-of-the-covenant

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Emphasizes the symbolic application to believers: "This is symbolic of God's choice today. Without His power, there is no difference among men. But God energizes His choice to fulfill His calling, and to bear fruit for Him, see John 15:1-8." The almond *shaked* means "the waker" — first to waken from winter's sleep. The miracle confirmed that "as Aaron's rod could not blossom and bear fruit by nature, so there was no more power inherent in Aaron than in any of the other 'princes' in Israel."
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-17.html

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Emphasizes the supernatural, miraculous nature and the pastoral lesson that God's chosen leaders are not the most spiritual but are appointed by God. The rod had "both fruit (the almond) and the promise of future fruit" — a mark of election.
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

---

## v. 9 — "Then Moses brought out all the staffs from the LORD's presence to all the Israelites. They saw them, and each man took his own staff."

Each prince took back his own rod and saw for himself that it remained "dry and barren as they were by nature, while Aaron's had been made to live" (Pulpit Commentary). This was a dramatic public verification — no room for doubt or accusation of trickery.
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds: "The text implies that careful inspection was made of each rod. This confirmed the miracle and God's choice."
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-17.html

Guzik: "We can imagine Moses carefully inspecting the other rods, noting that there was nothing on them resembling a sprout, bud, or blossom." The difference "could be attributed to God alone. It was a miracle that only God could do. This should have made Aaron humbler."
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

---

## v. 10 — "Put Aaron's staff back in front of the Testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebellious, so that you may put an end to their grumbling against Me, lest they die."

God commanded the rod to be preserved as a permanent witness. The Pulpit Commentary notes that "before the testimony" (v. 7) means before the ark; but Hebrews 9:4 says the rod was *in* the ark. The Pulpit suggests that after inspection by the princes, "it was deposited for safer preservation and easier conveyance inside the sacred chest." By Solomon's time it had disappeared (1 Kings 8:9). The rod could serve as a token only as long as it retained evidence of having sprouted — "either miraculously in a fresh state, or naturally in a withered state." Since the lesson never needed to be learned again, "we may suppose that the rod was left first to shrivel with age, and then to be lost through some accident."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

**Constable** concurs: "There is no reason to believe that the buds, blossoms, and fruits remained perpetually fresh. They probably wilted and the rod most likely assumed the condition it had before the miracle."
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-17.html

**Enduring Word (Guzik)** provides a striking theological insight about the ark's contents: "Aaron's rod was to be kept in the ark of the covenant, as another example of Israel's failure and rebellion. When God looked down from heaven into the ark, He saw emblems of Israel's sin: The tablets of the law that they broke, the manna that they complained about, and Aaron's rod which was the answer to their rebellion. The covering blood of sacrifice was applied to the lid covering over these reminders of Israel's sin, so God 'saw' the blood 'covering' their sin, and atonement was made."
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

The Hebrew phrase is literally "children of rebellion" (Pulpit Commentary, cf. Ephesians 2:2-3). God states the murmuring is ultimately "against Me" — a complaint against God's appointed leaders is a complaint against God Himself (Guzik).
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

**Haydock / Catholic:** "It was not the rod with which so many miracles had been wrought" (Tirinus). Tostat (a medieval commentator) believed the rod remained perpetually in its budded state while in the ark: "'The grace of the priesthood never fades' (St. Ambrose, ep. 63)."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/17.htm

---

## v. 11 — "So Moses did as the LORD had commanded him."

Moses' simple obedience is recorded. The note is brief across all commentaries — a straightforward report of compliance.

---

## v. 12 — "Then the Israelites declared to Moses, 'Look, we are perishing! We are lost; we are all lost!'"

The Pulpit Commentary offers a vivid description: "These are the last wailings of the great storm which had raged against Moses and Aaron… which was now sobbing itself out in the petulant despair of defeated and disheartened men, cowed indeed, but not convinced, fearful to offend, yet not loving to obey."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

**Guzik** observes that they were "clearly convicted of their sin." They now knew it was wrong to contest Aaron's priestly leadership. Yet "this kind of feverish fear doesn't necessarily mean their hearts were changed. This will not be the last account of a complaining, murmuring Israel. This shows that dramatic events don't take away our complaining and rebelliousness. The heart must be changed by God." He also cites Adam Clarke suggesting the Hebrew *gavaenu* describes "an extreme difficulty of breathing, which, producing suffocation, ends at last in death" — the shortness of breath that comes with panic.
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

**Haydock** notes: "Many had been already destroyed. Those who remained, and were conscious of their seditious practices, feared a similar treatment."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/17.htm

---

## v. 13 — "Anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD will die. Are we all going to perish?"

The people's terror was understandable given the recent judgments: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram swallowed by the earth; 250 leaders consumed by fire; 14,700 killed by plague (chapter 16). The Pulpit Commentary says their question — "Shall we be consumed with dying?" — could only be answered in the affirmative, for their sentence was already pronounced: "In this wilderness they shall be consumed" (Numbers 14:35). "But it was not in human nature that they should calmly accept their fate."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/17.htm

**Constable** notes: "The people's terror probably arose as a result of the miracles and judgments that had befallen the Israelites since Korah rebelled. God had vindicated His holiness, the people realized their sinfulness, and they were full of fear."
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-17.html

**Haydock** observes that some commentators believe the people "were now entering into themselves, and desirous to know what they must do to escape the fate of their brethren. God gives them an answer in the following chapter, teaching them that they must refrain from approaching to the tabernacle, unless they be authorized; and provide such things as are requisite for the maintenance of those whom he has chosen for his ministers." Haydock also notes that after chapter 17, Scripture "passes over the transactions of about 35 years, in profound silence, that the memory of those who had so often murmured, might perish."
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/17.htm

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds: "This holy awe apparently remained with them for many generations."
https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-17.html

**Morgan** (cited by Guzik): "The sign was efficacious; for while the spirit of rebellion manifested itself subsequently in other ways, it may safely be said that any complaint against the rights of the God-appointed priesthood ceased from this time."
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-17/

---

## Summary of Denominational Distinctives

| Tradition | Distinctive Emphasis |
|---|---|
| **Catholic** (Haydock/Challoner) | Aaron's budding rod is a type of the Virgin Mary (virginal conception) and of Christ's passion/resurrection. The Fathers (Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory of Nyssa, Bernard) are cited. |
| **Reformed** (Ligonier) | The rod in the ark demonstrates God's *sovereign choice* of the priestly mediator; the ark as a whole pictures Christ's person and saving work (Heb 5:4). |
| **Baptist** (Garner-Howes) | Emphasizes the practical parallel: just as God energized a dead rod, He energizes His chosen people today to bear fruit (John 15). Stresses the miracle as confirming God's choice of a specific line. |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Guzik) | Highlights the supernatural, miraculous nature; God gave "more than enough evidence." Emphasizes that God's choice is not about personal merit and that dramatic signs don't change hearts — only God can. |
| **Evangelical (broad)** (Precept Austin, Constable) | Focuses on the word study (*matteh*), the almond symbolism (vigilance), and the cessation of murmuring against the priesthood. The rod as evidence of divine appointment in life — fruit-bearing proves authority but humbles. |
| **Older Anglican/Conservative** (Pulpit, Ellicott) | Rich in Hebrew word studies, historical context, and Christological typology (Christ as the shoot from Jesse's stem). The Pulpit's psychological reading of vv. 12-13 as "petulant despair" is distinctive. |
